    AI Overview
    humiliation
    /hyo͞oˌmilēˈāSHən/
    Humiliation is
    the intense, painful experience of losing self-esteem, dignity, or status, often caused by the unjust, public exercise of power by others. It differs from shame by centering on being wronged rather than doing wrong, often causing intense anger and a "freezing" trauma response. 
    Coping and Overcoming Humiliation 
    • Cultivate Self-Compassion: Develop a compassionate, "compassionate self" identity (wise, strong, courageous) to counter feelings of worthlessness, as explained by Dr. Paul Gilbert's work on Compassion and Self-Compassion.
    • Shift Perspective: Recognize that humiliation is often an external, unfair power move, allowing you to assign responsibility to the perpetrator rather than internalizing the shame
      .
    • Somatic Regulation: Use breathing exercises, upright posture, and friendly facial expressions to activate the parasympathetic nervous system and move out of a "freeze" state.
    • Process the Emotion: Acknowledge the anger and desire for revenge without acting on it, transforming it into proactive, positive action. 
    Role of Humiliation in Social Interactions 
    • Exercise of Power: Humiliation is a tool used to demonstrate superiority, resulting in the exclusion or silencing of individuals or groups.
    • Discipline and Shame: Historically and occasionally in modern times, it is used as a public mechanism to punish wrongdoing, such as public shaming, as seen in this Wikipedia article on Public humiliation.
    • Social Disruption: It causes significant negative social consequences, including decreased trust, social isolation, and potential for violent retaliation. 
    Common Forms 
    • Public Failures: Being embarrassed publicly, rejected, betrayed, or having failures highlighted.
    • Status Reduction: Being treated as worthless, ignored, or having one's competence doubted.
    • Abuse of Power: Physical or verbal violations, including being forced into humiliating acts.

    Coping Strategies. How can one cope with or overcome humiliation?
    About this result
    Feedback
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    Coping with humiliation involves acknowledging the pain without judgment, practicing self-compassion, and separating your self-worth from the event. To move forward, take accountability if necessary, learn from the experience, and set boundaries to avoid future situations. Overcoming it requires time, resilience, and often, support from others. 
    Key Strategies for Coping and Overcoming:
    • Acknowledge and Own the Feeling:
      Don't let your mind twist the incident into something fictional; acknowledge what happened, but refuse to let it define you. Label the emotion without judging yourself, as suggested in a post on Rula. 
    • Put it in Perspective:
      Realize that most humiliating moments are temporary and not as personal as they feel. Most people are focused on their own lives and will forget the incident quickly. 
    • Use Humour or Vulnerability:
      If possible, laughing at yourself can disarm the humiliation and take the tension out of the situation. 
    • Learn and Adapt:
      Treat the event as a lesson, not a life sentence. Identify what you can do differently if a similar situation arises. 
    • Seek Support and Set Boundaries:
      Talk to trusted friends or a therapist to process the trauma and build resilience. Set firm boundaries with people who continue to make you feel uncomfortable. 
    • Practice Self-Compassion:
      Forgive yourself if the mistake was yours. Remember that mistakes are a part of being human. 
    If the humiliation is causing lasting trauma, therapy (like DBT or cognitive-behavioral techniques) can be helpful in addressing deep-seated shame.
